input.vignette:
A 4-month-old male infant is evaluated during a routine well-child check. The parents report difficulty weaning him from nighttime feedings, noting that he becomes extremely distressed after 3-4 hours without feeding and is only consoled by being fed.

Growth assessment reveals a decline from the 25th to the 5th percentile in length, while weight remains at the 25th percentile. Physical examination reveals distinctive facial fullness, significantly distended abdomen, and thin limbs. The liver edge extends to the iliac crest, but the spleen is not enlarged.

A blood sample demonstrates a characteristic milky white layer on its surface.

Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

Options:
A. Prader-Willi syndrome
B. Congenital hyperinsulinism
C. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
E. Gaucher disease
F. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
G. Glycogen storage disease type 1
H. Tay-Sachs disease
I. Familial hypercholesterolemia
J. Niemann-Pick disease type A

knowledge_chunks.title: Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia. > Low serum PTH > Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia
knowledge_chunks.text: Between the 1930s and 1950s, there was an increase in reported cases of hypercalcaemia in children by clinicians in the UK. Initial observations included failure to thrive, hypercalcaemia and distinct facial features (described as “elfin”). While the hypercalcaemia was transient in some, the facial abnormalities, developmental delay and mental retardation persisted. In 1953, Lightwood and Stapleton suggested that a distinction should be made between those individuals with “syndromic” hypercalcaemia accompanied by distinct facial features and mental retardation, and those with classical features of hypercalcaemia, including thirst, dehydration and polyuria. This latter milder form was termed idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia (IIH, OMIM #143880), and the former named Williams-Beuren Syndrome (see next section). The increased prevalence of IIH in the 1950s in the UK was linked to the high dose of vitamin D fortification in milk and cereals, an initiative that had begun to prevent rickets in the population. An oversensitivity to vitamin D was suggested to be the cause of hypercalcaemia in those individuals with IIH.

knowledge_chunks.title: Pediatric Feeding Disorder: Consensus Definition and Conceptual Framework. > History and Physical
knowledge_chunks.text: For infants, the medical and nutritional history should include prenatal and birth details, including maternal health conditions, labor and delivery complications, mode of delivery, gestational age, congenital anomalies, respiratory or neurological disorders, prior hospitalizations, and any use of feeding tubes or specialized formulas. The feeding skills history should evaluate developmental milestones related to feeding (eg, transitioning from purees to solids), oral-motor coordination, and any history of choking, vomiting, or regurgitation, which may suggest an anatomic obstruction or motility disorder. Food refusal may be a sign of food allergy, food intolerance, or sensory aversion. A caregiver's history is also vital, focusing on the type of feeding, techniques, and positioning used while feeding the infant.[9]

knowledge_chunks.title: International clinical guideline for the management of classical galactosemia: diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. > Introduction
knowledge_chunks.text: Galactosemia is an inborn error of metabolism due to impaired degradation of galactose. The disease was first described in 1917, and defective galactose metabolism was explained as the cause in the 1950s. If not recognized and treated promptly, affected infants may develop significant morbidity within days of birth. Newborn screening tests in developed countries have helped identify affected infants early. However, providers must maintain a high index of suspicion in ill newborns as feeding intolerance, hepatomegaly, lethargy, coagulopathy, and renal dysfunction may occur within the first few days of life, even before newborn screening tests have been finalized.[1][2][3]

knowledge_chunks.title: Approach to the Patient With Pancreatogenic Diabetes. > Causes of Pancreatitis and PPDM
knowledge_chunks.text: Hypertriglyceridemia is the third leading cause of AP in both adults and pediatrics. AP risk increases when serum triglycerides are 1000 mg/dL or higher and is less likely to occur when serum triglycerides are below 500 mg/dL. A 4% increase in AP incidence is reported for every 100 mg/dL of triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL. Hypertriglyceridemia can result from genetics, disease conditions, medications, and combinations of these. Poorly controlled diabetes, obesity, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, HIV infection, lipodystrophy, alcohol, oral estrogen, and glucocorticoid are factors that increase serum triglycerides levels. In addition, pregnancy causes a physiological increase in triglycerides that can trigger AP in rare cases. Management of hypertriglyceridemia by addressing contributing factors, ceasing alcohol use, and reducing carbohydrate intake is important to prevent the recurrence of pancreatitis. Fenofibrates and omega-3 fatty acids may be utilized to treat those whose triglyceride levels do not respond sufficiently to lifestyle modification and the removal of offending factors.
